Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Name: engine-v2-1
  - Namespace: canary-deployment-ns
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no additional securityContext)

- Updated Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (ClusterIP)
  - Selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Port unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Result
- Both stable (engine-v2-0) and canary (engine-v2-1) pods are endpoints behind the Service:
  - Endpoints show 4 addresses: 2 from v2.0 and 2 from v2.1
  - With equal endpoints, traffic will be approximately 50/50 between stable and canary

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Optional: run a temporary curl pod and send repeated requests to observe headers/body/version

Adjusting or rolling back
- To shift traffic, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary to 1 for ~33%, to 3 for ~60%, etc.)
- To roll back to stable-only, update the Service selector back to:
  selector:
    app: recommendation-engine
    version: v2.0
  or scale down/delete engine-v2-1.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Name: engine-v2-1
  - Namespace: canary-deployment-ns
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no additional securityContext)

- Updated Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (ClusterIP)
  - Selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Port unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Result
- Both stable (engine-v2-0) and canary (engine-v2-1) pods are endpoints behind the Service:
  - Endpoints show 4 addresses: 2 from v2.0 and 2 from v2.1
  - With equal endpoints, traffic will be approximately 50/50 between stable and canary

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Optional: run a temporary curl pod and send repeated requests to observe headers/body/version

Adjusting or rolling back
- To shift traffic, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary to 1 for ~33%, to 3 for ~60%, etc.)
- To roll back to stable-only, update the Service selector back to:
  selector:
    app: recommendation-engine
    version: v2.0
  or scale down/delete engine-v2-1.

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Name: engine-v2-1
  - Namespace: canary-deployment-ns
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no additional securityContext)

- Updated Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (ClusterIP)
  - Selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Port unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Result
- Both stable (engine-v2-0) and canary (engine-v2-1) pods are endpoints behind the Service:
  - Endpoints show 4 addresses: 2 from v2.0 and 2 from v2.1
  - With equal endpoints, traffic will be approximately 50/50 between stable and canary

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Optional: run a temporary curl pod and send repeated requests to observe headers/body/version

Adjusting or rolling back
- To shift traffic, change replica counts (e.g., scale canary to 1 for ~33%, to 3 for ~60%, etc.)
- To roll back to stable-only, update the Service selector back to:
  selector:
    app: recommendation-engine
    version: v2.0
  or scale down/delete engine-v2-1.

- Ingress is unaffected (policyTypes: Egress)

I fixed the CrashLoopBackOff in Deployment app (namespace crashloop-test).

What was wrong
- The container was starting with args: ["nonexistent_command"], causing the pod to crash.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the bad args.

Steps.message:
I fixed the CrashLoopBackOff in Deployment app (namespace crashloop-test).

What was wrong
- The container was starting with args: ["nonexistent_command"], causing the pod to crash.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the bad args.
- Set the container to run nginx with the proper startup:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
  - containerPort: 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080)

Current status
- Pod app-59b44cb8f7-b4m5r is 1/1 Running with 0 restarts.
- Old crashing pod was terminated; the new ReplicaSet is healthy.

If you want, I can add a Service to expose it or readiness/liveness probes for better health checks.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed the CrashLoopBackOff in Deployment app (namespace crashloop-test).

What was wrong
- The container was starting with args: ["nonexistent_command"], causing the pod to crash.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the bad args.
- Set the container to run nginx with the proper startup:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
  - containerPort: 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080)

Current status
- Pod app-59b44cb8f7-b4m5r is 1/1 Running with 0 restarts.
- Old crashing pod was terminated; the new ReplicaSet is healthy.

If you want, I can add a Service to expose it or readiness/liveness probes for better health checks.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it. Summary:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the PVC stayed unbound and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- Fix applied:
  - Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (spec is immutable).
  - Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).
  - The external provisioner created and bound a PV to the PVC.
- Result: The pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is started and healthy.

Useful checks:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pvc homepage-pvc

If you intended to use a different storage class than “standard,” tell me the correct one and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it. Summary:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the PVC stayed unbound and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- Fix applied:
  - Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (spec is immutable).
  - Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).
  - The external provisioner created and bound a PV to the PVC.
- Result: The pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is started and healthy.

Useful checks:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pvc homepage-pvc

If you intended to use a different storage class than “standard,” tell me the correct one and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it. Summary:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the PVC stayed unbound and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- Fix applied:
  - Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (spec is immutable).
  - Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (the default StorageClass available in your cluster).
  - The external provisioner created and bound a PV to the PVC.
- Result: The pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is started and healthy.

Useful checks:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pvc homepage-pvc

If you intended to use a different storage class than “standard,” tell me the correct one and I can switch the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 at /get_status and /is_ready (paths that don’t exist), causing readiness/liveness failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (keeps Service port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available (1/1).
- Pod is Ready (1/1).
- Service orders/webapp is ClusterIP on port 80 -> container port 8080.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster: kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://webapp
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to expose it externally (Ingress/LoadBalancer) and set up a hostname? If yes, tell me the host/domain you’d like to use.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 at /get_status and /is_ready (paths that don’t exist), causing readiness/liveness failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (keeps Service port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available (1/1).
- Pod is Ready (1/1).
- Service orders/webapp is ClusterIP on port 80 -> container port 8080.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster: kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://webapp
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to expose it externally (Ingress/LoadBalancer) and set up a hostname? If yes, tell me the host/domain you’d like to use.

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 at /get_status and /is_ready (paths that don’t exist), causing readiness/liveness failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (keeps Service port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available (1/1).
- Pod is Ready (1/1).
- Service orders/webapp is ClusterIP on port 80 -> container port 8080.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster: kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://webapp
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to expose it externally (Ingress/LoadBalancer) and set up a hostname? If yes, tell me the host/domain you’d like to use.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the pod-reader service account lacked permission to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""] (core)
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Left the existing deployments list permission intact. The RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note: This grants access only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the pod-reader service account lacked permission to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""] (core)
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Left the existing deployments list permission intact. The RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note: This grants access only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the pod-reader service account lacked permission to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""] (core)
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Left the existing deployments list permission intact. The RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note: This grants access only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pods. Service nginx had selector app=web while the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx. That left the Service with no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- Ports are correct: the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, and the Service maps port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods (app=nginx).

Current state (key facts)
- Service web/nginx: ClusterIP 10.97.151.89, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx.
- Endpoints populated: 10.244.0.27:8080 (nginx-6d94b64d45-kj5p2). Traffic should now flow.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster (any Pod), curl one of:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - http://nginx
  - http://10.97.151.89
- Example command you can run:
  - kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- curl -sI http://nginx

Note on external access
- The Service type is ClusterIP (internal only). If you’re trying to reach nginx from outside the cluster, expose it via:
  - NodePort (quick): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort","ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
  - Ingress/LoadBalancer (preferred in prod): create an Ingress or set type: LoadBalancer (if supported).

Want me to expose it externally (and which method)?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pods. Service nginx had selector app=web while the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx. That left the Service with no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- Ports are correct: the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, and the Service maps port 80 -> targetPort 8080.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods (app=nginx).

Current state (key facts)
- Service web/nginx: ClusterIP 10.97.151.89, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx.
- Endpoints populated: 10.244.0.27:8080 (nginx-6d94b64d45-kj5p2). Traffic should now flow.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster (any Pod), curl one of:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - http://nginx
  - http://10.97.151.89
- Example command you can run:
  - kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- curl -sI http://nginx

Note on external access
- The Service type is ClusterIP (internal only). If you’re trying to reach nginx from outside the cluster, expose it via:
  - NodePort (quick): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort","ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
  - Ingress/LoadBalancer (preferred in prod): create an Ingress or set type: LoadBalancer (if supported).

Want me to expose it externally (and which method)?

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings and fixes

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. Scheduler error: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Connection refused: The nginx container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. So traffic to web-app-service:80 was forwarded to a non-listening port on the pods.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - Node mcp-eval-cluster now has label environment=production-gpu.
  - Result: Pods scheduled and started running.
- Corrected the Service to match the container’s listening port:
  - Updated web-app-service targetPort from 80 to 8080.

Current status (verified)
- Pods are Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-795tz: Running, IP 10.244.0.31
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-sqg4j: Running, IP 10.244.0.30
- Service endpoints are healthy and on the right port:
  - web-app-service Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080, 10.244.0.31:8080
- With these fixes, web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will now map to pod port 8080 and should no longer return connection refused.

Summary of findings and fixes

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. Scheduler error: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Connection refused: The nginx container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. So traffic to web-app-service:80 was forwarded to a non-listening port on the pods.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - Node mcp-eval-cluster now has label environment=production-gpu.
  - Result: Pods scheduled and started running.
- Corrected the Service to match the container’s listening port:
  - Updated web-app-service targetPort from 80 to 8080.

- Pods are Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-795tz: Running, IP 10.244.0.31

- Service endpoints are healthy and on the right port:
  - web-app-service Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080, 10.244.0.31:8080
- With these fixes, web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will now map to pod port 8080 and should no longer return connection refused.

Notes and recommendations
- If labeling the node is not desired (since it’s a cluster-wide change), I can instead remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can run on any schedulable node.
- For clarity, consider updating the Deployment’s containerPort to 8080 to match the actual nginx listen port (containerPort is informational but helps avoid confusion).

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings and fixes

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. Scheduler error: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Connection refused: The nginx container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. So traffic to web-app-service:80 was forwarded to a non-listening port on the pods.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - Node mcp-eval-cluster now has label environment=production-gpu.
  - Result: Pods scheduled and started running.
- Corrected the Service to match the container’s listening port:
  - Updated web-app-service targetPort from 80 to 8080.

Current status (verified)
- Pods are Running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-795tz: Running, IP 10.244.0.31
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-sqg4j: Running, IP 10.244.0.30
- Service endpoints are healthy and on the right port:
  - web-app-service Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080, 10.244.0.31:8080
- With these fixes, web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will now map to pod port 8080 and should no longer return connection refused.

Notes and recommendations
- If labeling the node is not desired (since it’s a cluster-wide change), I can instead remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can run on any schedulable node.
- For clarity, consider updating the Deployment’s containerPort to 8080 to match the actual nginx listen port (containerPort is informational but helps avoid confusion).
- Let me know if you want me to:
  - Remove the node label and update the Deployment to drop nodeSelector, or
  - Keep the node label and update the Deployment’s containerPort to 8080 for consistency.

            httpGet:

              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080

I have set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled dev namespaces with type=dev-tenant for easy targeting and policy scoping

2) RBAC
- Developer user access (adjust user names to match your IdP/CN as needed):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User alice
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User bob
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to Users alice, bob, charlie
- ServiceAccounts
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod access
  - No developer bindings in staging or prod. By default only cluster-admins (e.g., system:masters) or whoever you explicitly bind will have access

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, requests.cpu=2
  - limits.memory=4Gi, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I have set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled dev namespaces with type=dev-tenant for easy targeting and policy scoping

2) RBAC
- Developer user access (adjust user names to match your IdP/CN as needed):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User alice
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User bob
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to Users alice, bob, charlie
- ServiceAccounts
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod access
  - No developer bindings in staging or prod. By default only cluster-admins (e.g., system:masters) or whoever you explicitly bind will have access

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, requests.cpu=2
  - limits.memory=4Gi, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, requests.cpu=4
  - limits.memory=8Gi, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, requests.cpu=8
  - limits.memory=16Gi, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny
  - For dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod:
    - default-deny-ingress and default-deny-egress in each namespace
- Allow within namespace
  - allow-from-same-namespace (ingress) and allow-egress-same-namespace (egress) in each dev namespace and dev-shared
  - staging/prod also have allow-from-same-namespace for internal communication
- Devs can only access own namespace + dev-shared
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (egress) only
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-tenants (ingress) narrows inbound traffic to namespaces labeled type=dev-tenant
- DNS/system services
  - Per-namespace allow-dns egress rule to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53)
  - If you need additional “system services” (e.g., metrics-server or other kube-system pods) reachable, let me know and I’ll add a broader allow to kube-system as appropriate
- Staging/prod isolation
  - Staging/prod have default-deny ingress/egress plus DNS egress only and same-namespace ingress; there are no rules allowing any dev namespace to reach them

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all non-system namespaces created above (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) untouched

Notes and follow-ups
- User identities: The RoleBindings reference Users alice, bob, charlie. Update these subjects to match your cluster’s auth provider (e.g., OIDC usernames or groups). If you prefer group-based RBAC (e.g., group=dev-alice), I can switch to Groups for flexibility.
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - Example to get a short-lived token:
    - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token if you need a long-lived token.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRanges to set default requests/limits per namespace so workloads don’t get rejected by quotas and to control per-pod/container sizing by default.
  - If you want explicit staging/prod access for a specific admin group (beyond cluster-admin), we can add RoleBindings in those namespaces to your admin group(s).

Verification tips
- RBAC:
  - As alice, ensure full access only in dev-alice and read-only in dev-shared; no access to dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod
- Network isolation:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-bob should fail; curl a Service in dev-shared should succeed; DNS lookups should work
  - From dev namespaces, accessing staging/prod should fail
  - Within staging/prod, traffic is allowed only within each namespace and to DNS

If you need me to broaden “system services” access beyond DNS (e.g., allow egress to kube-system generally or specific system pods), or to tailor the RBAC subjects to your identity system, say the word and I’ll apply the changes.

outputSteps.content:
I have set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled dev namespaces with type=dev-tenant for easy targeting and policy scoping

2) RBAC
- Developer user access (adjust user names to match your IdP/CN as needed):
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User alice
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User bob
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding grants ClusterRole admin to User charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to Users alice, bob, charlie
- ServiceAccounts
  - Created alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole admin in its own namespace
  - Each SA bound to ClusterRole view in dev-shared
- Staging and prod access
  - No developer bindings in staging or prod. By default only cluster-admins (e.g., system:masters) or whoever you explicitly bind will have access

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, requests.cpu=2
  - limits.memory=4Gi, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, requests.cpu=4
  - limits.memory=8Gi, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, requests.cpu=8
  - limits.memory=16Gi, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny
  - For dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod:
    - default-deny-ingress and default-deny-egress in each namespace
- Allow within namespace
  - allow-from-same-namespace (ingress) and allow-egress-same-namespace (egress) in each dev namespace and dev-shared
  - staging/prod also have allow-from-same-namespace for internal communication
- Devs can only access own namespace + dev-shared
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (egress) only
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-tenants (ingress) narrows inbound traffic to namespaces labeled type=dev-tenant
- DNS/system services
  - Per-namespace allow-dns egress rule to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53)
  - If you need additional “system services” (e.g., metrics-server or other kube-system pods) reachable, let me know and I’ll add a broader allow to kube-system as appropriate
- Staging/prod isolation
  - Staging/prod have default-deny ingress/egress plus DNS egress only and same-namespace ingress; there are no rules allowing any dev namespace to reach them

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all non-system namespaces created above (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) untouched

Notes and follow-ups
- User identities: The RoleBindings reference Users alice, bob, charlie. Update these subjects to match your cluster’s auth provider (e.g., OIDC usernames or groups). If you prefer group-based RBAC (e.g., group=dev-alice), I can switch to Groups for flexibility.
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - Example to get a short-lived token:
    - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token if you need a long-lived token.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRanges to set default requests/limits per namespace so workloads don’t get rejected by quotas and to control per-pod/container sizing by default.
  - If you want explicit staging/prod access for a specific admin group (beyond cluster-admin), we can add RoleBindings in those namespaces to your admin group(s).

Verification tips
- RBAC:
  - As alice, ensure full access only in dev-alice and read-only in dev-shared; no access to dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod
- Network isolation:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-bob should fail; curl a Service in dev-shared should succeed; DNS lookups should work
  - From dev namespaces, accessing staging/prod should fail
  - Within staging/prod, traffic is allowed only within each namespace and to DNS

If you need me to broaden “system services” access beyond DNS (e.g., allow egress to kube-system generally or specific system pods), or to tailor the RBAC subjects to your identity system, say the word and I’ll apply the changes.
